data.title: Don't Ignore The Insider Selling In Moog
data.description:
Some Moog Inc. (NYSE:MOG.A) shareholders may be a little concerned to see that the Non-Executive Chairman, John Scannell, recently sold a substantial US$1.0m worth of stock at a price of US$346 per share. However, it's crucial to note that they remain very much invested in the stock and that sale only reduced their holding by 5.3%.

This technology could replace computers: discover the 20 stocks are working to make quantum computing a reality.

The Last 12 Months Of Insider Transactions At Moog

Notably, that recent sale by Non-Executive Chairman John Scannell was not the only time they sold Moog shares this year. They previously made an even bigger sale of -US$2.1m worth of shares at a price of US$232 per share. That means that even when the share price was below the current price of US$328, an insider wanted to cash in some shares. We generally consider it a negative if insiders have been selling, especially if they did so below the current price, because it implies that they considered a lower price to be reasonable. Please do note, however, that sellers may have a variety of reasons for selling, so we don't know for sure what they think of the stock price. It is worth noting that this sale was only 13% of John Scannell's holding.

John Scannell ditched 15.00k shares over the year. The average price per share was US$283. You can see the insider transactions (by companies and individuals) over the last year depicted in the chart below. If you click on the chart, you can see all the individual transactions, including the share price, individual, and the date!

See our latest analysis for Moog

I will like Moog better if I see some big insider buys. While we wait, check out this free list of undervalued and small cap stocks with considerable, recent, insider buying.

Does Moog Boast High Insider Ownership?

I like to look at how many shares insiders own in a company, to help inform my view of how aligned they are with insiders. A high insider ownership often makes company leadership more mindful of shareholder interests. Moog insiders own 1.1% of the company, currently worth about US$114m based on the recent share price. Most shareholders would be happy to see this sort of insider ownership, since it suggests that management incentives are well aligned with other shareholders.

So What Does This Data Suggest About Moog Insiders?

An insider sold stock recently, but they haven't been buying. And there weren't any purchases to give us comfort, over the last year. But it is good to see that Moog is growing earnings. It is good to see high insider ownership, but the insider selling leaves us cautious. So while it's helpful to know what insiders are doing in terms of buying or selling, it's also helpful to know the risks that a particular company is facing. To assist with this, we've discovered 1 warning sign that you should run your eye over to get a better picture of Moog.

Of course Moog may not be the best stock to buy. So you may wish to see this free collection of high quality companies.

For the purposes of this article, insiders are those individuals who report their transactions to the relevant regulatory body. We currently account for open market transactions and private dispositions of direct interests only, but not derivative transactions or indirect interests.

data.title: What Regeneron Pharmaceuticals Doubters Got Wrong
data.description:
Regeneron Pharmaceuticals spent this past year stacking fresh deals and clinical milestones, from the Telix radiopharmaceutical tie‑up to FDA approval of Livsayis for generalized myasthenia gravis. Investors who held Regeneron Pharmaceuticals over the past year are up 25.9%, including dividends. If you were deciding whether to buy on 19 November 2025, you would have seen that bullish and bearish analysts were 31% apart on fair value. Which story about Regeneron’s future did that spread really require you to accept?

This theme extends beyond Regeneron Pharmaceuticals. See which of 36 healthcare AI stocks may still merit a closer look.

The Two Stories Regeneron Investors Were Choosing Between

The shares cost US$703 at the start of the period, so anyone looking at Regeneron Pharmaceuticals then had to decide which of two very different stories to lean toward.

On the upbeat side, the bullish camp saw a Fair Value of US$921, a price implied by assumptions that Dupixent and EYLEA HD could capture far greater US and global market share. That view rested on expectations of 7.9% annual revenue growth and rising profit margins, helped by manufacturing expansion and a broader oncology and hematology portfolio.

The bearish narrative pointed to a Fair Value of US$540, a level based on the idea that biosimilars and US healthcare reforms would steadily erode pricing power. That scenario assumed revenue growth of only 1.4% a year and profit margins falling to 22.5%, with EYLEA and Dupixent exposure, rising R&D costs, and demographic shifts all pressuring future earnings.

What The Evidence Around Regeneron Actually Tested

Regeneron Pharmaceuticals secured FDA approval for Livsayis in generalized myasthenia gravis and reported Q3 2026 revenue of US$5,115.8m and net income of US$1,948.7m, both above Q3 2025 levels, which leaned toward the bullish growth story. Net margin slipped from 38.9% to 38.1%, and the failed melanoma trial with resulting class actions pushed back against the idea of steadily rising profitability. Overall, the evidence cut both ways.

The key assumption investors were really testing was whether product and partnership wins outpace pricing and pipeline setbacks. For another healthcare stock, you would track whether new approvals, trial readouts, and deal flow show up in higher sales and stable or improving net margin, rather than just in headlines.

What Regeneron’s Current Price Already Assumes

Regeneron Pharmaceuticals now trades at US$923 after a 25.9% gain over the past year. The bearish analyst Narrative on Simply Wall St places its Fair Value below that level, even while accepting strong recent execution across Dupixent, EYLEA HD and newer programs.

That Narrative hinges on whether fresh franchises and pipeline assets genuinely offset pricing, trial and legal pressures. A buyer at today’s price effectively assumes the current breadth of commercial performance and late stage drugs holds up. The question is how those risks affect that belief in durability.

"The main factor that has to go right is that Regeneron Pharmaceuticals converts its broad pipeline and newer franchises such as EYLEA HD, Libtayo, cemdisiran and Pasatru into durable earnings streams that offset pricing pressure and legal and regulatory risks."

One Narrative has put a figure on that disagreement. → See the Narrative with its lower Fair Value, assumptions and all

Another Healthcare Story Nearby

Regeneron keeps the focus on drug pipelines and trial readouts. Your next question is where similar pressures are playing out differently.

One large peer is also leaning harder into oncology, immunology and neuroscience. Management there is trying to tilt toward higher margin specialty treatments.

That same group is reshaping its medical device arm and carving out slower pieces. It is spending heavily on early stage deals that currently weigh on reported earnings.

The bet is that these therapies and platforms eventually justify that upfront hit. If the mix shift works, this could be a very different healthcare story to examine.

data.title: XPeng Fell 54% While Sales Rose
data.description:
XPeng just announced the rollout of China’s first mass-produced Robotaxi built entirely in house, a headline that seems tailor made for an autonomy and Physical AI story. Investors who held XPeng from the start of the year are down 54.1%, including dividends. If you were considering that decision on 1 January 2026, how should this mix of record deliveries, wider losses and new Robotaxi ambitions influence what you expect from the business in the future?

On Simply Wall St, a Narrative is an investor's thesis written down: the reasoning, plus the numbers it rests on. Run those numbers and you get an estimated Fair Value.

XPeng has already moved. Pinpoint other ways to investigate the theme among 90 robotics and automation stocks.

The Two XPeng Stories Investors Had To Weigh

The shares cost US$20.28 at the start of the period, and XPeng sat between two sharply different stories about where the business might head next.

On the optimistic side, one thesis put Fair Value at US$26.29, about 30% above the start price. This view hinged on revenue rising 31.6% a year and profit margin reaching 4.6% within three years.

The cautious view pointed to a Fair Value of US$18.06. It highlighted concern that global EV rivalry and trade barriers could keep pricing pressure intense and limit the benefits of international expansion.

What The XPeng Results Put To The Test

XPeng’s launch of a fully in house, mass produced Robotaxi and strong Q3 2026 deliveries and revenue supported the optimistic story about scale and Physical AI. The harder edge came from the numbers. Revenue in Q3 2026 was CNY 24,276.0m, yet the business still reported a larger loss of CNY 868.0m and net margin fell to 3.6%. The evidence cut both ways.

The lesson is clear. When a thesis leans on future profitability, do not stop at delivery or revenue guidance. Track whether net losses shrink and whether net margin actually moves toward the level the story assumes.

What XPeng's Price Slide Now Asks You To Believe

XPeng trades at US$9.38 from the start of the year, leaving shareholders down 54.1% over that stretch. The bullish analyst Narrative on Simply Wall St still places its Fair Value above that quote, built on Physical AI and robotics sitting on top of the existing auto operation.

That view leans on one central test. A buyer today would be assuming XPeng can turn its Physical AI and overseas rollout into higher margin revenue that eventually outweighs the current losses and heavy research spend.

"Bullish analysts expect XPeng to turn its Physical AI platform of smart EVs, humanoid robots, and Robotaxis into a larger and structurally more profitable business as high-margin robotics and software subscriptions scale on top of the auto base. The main thing that has to go right is XPeng executing on global expansion in both vehicles and Physical AI, including successful overseas production ramp-up and commercial deployment of humanoid robots and Robotaxis while controlling rising R&D and operating costs."

One Narrative has put a figure on that disagreement. → See the Narrative with its higher Fair Value, assumptions and all

XPeng And A Different AI Bet

XPeng is pitching Physical AI through Robotaxis and humanoid plans, raising fresh questions. You could also look at a rival chasing a broader labour platform.

Instead of focusing on cars first, this other business is rebuilding its lines around general purpose robots. It wants machines that work across factories, homes and services.

The pitch is simple. Sell the robot once, then keep selling new skills through software licenses and monthly modules.

Where XPeng leans on vehicles plus autonomy, this path leans on robots plus recurring digital work. If that labour layer grows, the economics could look very different.
